articles.title: The Moirai at Velousia – Evia
articles.author: Τίτος Γιοχαλάς
articles.excerpt: A story from Velousia in Evia about the Moirai and their power to determine the fate of people...

image.alt: Traditional depiction of the Moirai at Velousia in Evia

content.value: People heard and believed in the Moirai. A woman gave birth, she had a girl, and her mother-in-law did not sleep for three nights. She did not sleep. And she heard the Moirai; the three Moirai came, and from one she heard that the girl who was born would reach the age of twelve and would go to drown herself in the Well of Hatzis.

But she did not tell the daughter-in-law. She told her son. She said to him:

"Come here, my son. This is what I heard from the Moirai. When the girl turns twelve, go and seal the well from above."

The father indeed went and sealed the well. But the girl, who was herding the cows, wandered over and went to the well.

She went round and round the well and burst. She died.

Then they went there and found the girl dead. Because she was destined to drown there and she did not find the well open. And since she found it sealed, she burst. She went round and round it and burst.

articles.title: The Moirai at Arachova
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk description of the Moirai as three old women who visit houses with newborns

content.value: The Moirai are three old women with large teeth, and they always walk together, bundled up. They anger easily. They always enter at night the house where there is a newborn baby; sometimes they also enter during the day, but only when the new mother is sleeping and no one else is present.

articles.title: The Moirai at Aegina
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk narrative about the Moirai and the ritual allotment of newborns' fate in Aegina

content.value: The Moirai are three sisters, and they dwell at the edge of the world, in a great and rich palace surrounded by a beautiful garden. They often come down to it, playing instruments and singing. They are like other women, except that they never die. They do all the housework themselves, and the garments they wear, they make themselves: they spin, they weave on a golden loom, and they sew them themselves.
Others say they do not live in a palace, but that each one has her own little house at the edge of the world, and that the houses are far apart from each other.

Still others say that at the edge of the world there are two great caves, far apart from each other, where the Moirai live — sometimes in one, sometimes in the other. Inside, these caves are finer than the richest house. And in the middle of each there is always a table laid with every kind of delicacy.

Often the Moirai leave their dwelling and wander all over the earth, to allot the fate of newborns. They allot the fate on the third day, and everyone knows this; so they prepare the child and tidy the house to receive the Moirai, and place in the middle of the room where the new mother lies a table with three seats. On the table they have honey and three almond kernels and three small spoons, three glasses of water, and three small candles. And they do all they can to please the Moirai and allot a good fate to the child.

When the Moirai come to the house where they will allot the child's fate, they are adorned, dressed in white, with a crown or some other ornament on their heads, with pearl necklaces at their throats and pearl bracelets. The eldest also holds a string of pearl worry-beads in her hand. She also has a book, and in it she writes down whatever all three allot to the child.

They enter the new mother's room at midnight. The eldest goes first, and all three sit at the table, with the eldest in the middle. After they rest, they eat the sweet and wish that the child too may be sweet and blessed all its life. Then the two younger ones deliberate on the child's fortunes, and if the eldest accepts them, she writes them in her book.

Many say that the Moirai who go to allot the child's fate carry — the eldest a pair of scissors, another a spindle, and the third a distaff with flax — and with these they determine how long it will live. At the allotting, one spins with the distaff, another winds the thread with the spindle, and each winding counts as one year. When the allotment is done, the eldest cuts the thread with her scissors. If the thread breaks before the allotting is finished, the Moirai stop and leave. And the child will live as many years as there are windings on the spindle, and whatever the Moirai managed to allot will come to pass.

articles.title: The Moirai at Amfissa
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk tradition about encountering the Moirai at the fountains of Amfissa on New Year's Eve

content.value: The Moirai go at night, before dawn, to the fountains and bathe and comb their golden hair, which reaches down to their knees.

For this reason, those who go to the fountain on New Year's Eve at night to fetch silent water — to drink at home on New Year's Day — take with them a plate of sweets, and after sprinkling them with water, they leave them on the stones near the fountain, so that the Moirai may eat when they come and be pleased and remain sweet and honey-like all year.
If anyone speaks while going to fetch the water, the Moirai will do them harm.

articles.title: The Moirai at Sitaria of Evros
articles.author: Ανάργυρος Εσκιτζόγλου
articles.excerpt: Description of beliefs about the Moirai (fate-giving deities) and rituals to appease them in Sitaria, Evros.

content.value: Everyone believes in the existence of the Moirai. "Each person has their own." The Moirai comes on the third day after the birth of the child and "allots its fate", i.e., determines whether it will turn out good or bad.
To appease the Moirai they undertake various actions, such as not crossing the path of unmarried people, placing lucky charms, and so on.
On the third day after the birth of the infant they make sweets to sweeten the Moirai.
